newsitem.title: USA: NYMEX crude, prods end up on weather, technicals.
newsitem.headline: NYMEX crude, prods end up on weather, technicals.

text.p: A combination of options expiry and a forecast for cold weather in the eastern U.S. lifted NYMEX crude and product futures, but analysts generally saw the market still in weak mode.

January crude futures gained 72 cents on the day to settle at $24.44 a barrel, making up about half the losses posted early in the week. Heating oil led the way, rising 3.04 cents to 71.71 cents a gallon, mainly on the weather report.
"We saw heating oil break that 71 area, led basically by reports of cooler temperatures," said Corey Bell, an analyst at brokerage Dean Witter.
"It was a continuation of the technical recovery we saw (Wednesday) but it is not out of hot water yet," said Bell.

According to widely-watched Smith Barney forecaster Jon Davis, "all indications point to an extended period of cold weather for much of the nation from the Rockies to the East Coast," starting next month and running through the end of December.

However, analysts and traders said that the prospect of cold weather on its own, though it may give temporary relief to the market, should not be enough to outweigh the negative factors which knocked nine pct off crude and products prices early in the week.
"People were getting pretty excited about this cold weather coming in...but it is pretty hard to read (the market) from here," said Tom Bentz, a trader at ING Derivatives.

He noted that there have been previous cold spells and a number weeks of above-normal temperatures in the past couple of months and the net result has been rising production and inventories of key products like heating oil.
"In products, we've seen two weeks of consistant builds in heating oil inventories and record production and inventory in gasoline," said Bell of Dean Witter.

For crude, "the real key feature is that we will have additional Iraqi oil on the world market shortly and overwhelmingly that should be bearish." He was referring to the resumption of Iraqi oil exports after six years under the United Nations "oil-for-food" deal, which is likely to see the first of a permitted $2 billion of exports over a six-month period hit the market over the weekend.

Meanwhile, the January crude contract has made a 50 percent retracement of the losses early in the week and Bentz pointed out that the final "gaps" on crude and products were filled in the final fifteen minutes of trading, probably linked to expiring options.

The January gasoline contract advanced 2.32 cents to end at 67.04 cents a gallon, despite news that Tosco Corp was taking steps to bring back on line the cat cracker at its Bayway, New Jersey refinery, down because of a glitch and small fire on Wednesday night.
"Today's market underscores how much the advance from Wednesday's low is unrelated to fundamental news," said Tim Evans of Thomson's Pegasus Econometrics.

"As in the rest of the complex, we think the gasoline market's longer-term agenda is a bearish one and that a retest of 62.80 is likely to confirm support even if the market has more work to do before breaking down again."
